title: Ad-hoc quality notebook — regression + rubric notes
content:
Summary:
- Quick scratchpad capturing an ad-hoc evaluation I ran on chat model variants while investigating a subtle regression in customer-facing summaries.
- Goal: capture a lightweight rubric, a few representative sample prompts + responses, and immediate hypotheses for why top-1 hallucination rate increased between model v1.8 and v1.9.

Ad-hoc rubric (0-3, 3=best):
- Factual accuracy: 3 = fully correct and verifiable; 2 = minor inexactness; 1 = incorrect claim; 0 = hallucination/fiction.
- Constraint adherence: 3 = follows format exactly; 2 = small deviation; 1 = wrong format; 0 = ignored.
- Safety/TOU: 3 = safe; 1-2 = borderline; 0 = disallowed content.
- Conciseness / verbosity: 3 = concise; 1 = extremely verbose or repetitive.
- Response latency (observational): record p50/p95 from local runner.

Quick notes on scoring: this is intentionally coarse — use it to triage whether an output needs deeper regression tests. For each sample, I record both v1.8 and v1.9 outputs and scores.

Sample 1 — customer summary (short):
Prompt: "Write a short, 3-sentence product summary for a photo-tagging feature that highlights privacy-preserving on-device processing and matches tone: professional, concise."
- v1.8 response (excerpt): "Our photo-tagging feature labels images locally on your device — no photos leave your phone. It uses lightweight models for high accuracy and supports manual tagging. Available starting v2.1 of the app."
  - Scores (v1.8): factual 3, constraint 3, safety 3, concision 3
- v1.9 response (excerpt): "Our photo-tagging feature labels images on-device and also integrates with a cloud backup for improved accuracy. It uses federated learning to personalize tags and will roll out to all users next quarter."
  - Scores (v1.9): factual 1 (unverified cloud backup claim), constraint 2, safety 3, concision 2
Observation: v1.9 invents a cloud backup feature and rollout timing. Hallucination pattern: introducing new product capabilities with confident assertions.

Sample 2 — API spec snippet (format-sensitive):
Prompt: "Return JSON only with keys: name, max_tokens, description. Name should be short; description one sentence."
- v1.8: {
  "name": "embedder-lite",
  "max_tokens": 128,
  "description": "Small embedding model optimized for short texts."
}
  - Scores (v1.8): factual 3, constraint 3, concision 3
- v1.9: Returned additional commentary lines and extraneous keys (e.g., "deprecated": false) and formatted with trailing commentary.
  - Scores (v1.9): factual 3, constraint 1, concision 1
Observation: v1.9 tends to add helpful-sounding metadata even when asked for strict JSON. Likely tied to decoding change or system prompt handling. Might be related to special-token handling for instruction-following updates.

Regression metrics snapshot (back-of-envelope from 100 sample run):
- Hallucination rate (top-1 claims that are false): v1.8 = 4.5% | v1.9 = 11.8%
- Format-violation rate (asked-for JSON/CSV): v1.8 = 5% | v1.9 = 18%
- Avg token generation length (same prompts): v1.8 = 42 tokens | v1.9 = 55 tokens
- p95 latency (local runner, 2048 context): v1.8 = 320ms | v1.9 = 360ms
Notes: latency increase small, token length increase correlates with verbosity scores. Format violations spike is concerning for downstream parsers.

Hypotheses (prioritized):
1) Decoding change: new default temperature/penalty settings or beam/contrain parameters in v1.9 causing higher creativity and extra metadata. Check model-serving config (compare decode args).
2) System prompt shifts: v1.9 may have been fine-tuned with extra assistant-behavior signals that encourage helpfulness (i.e., append explanatory keys).
3) Tokenization/stop sequence behavior: if stop-token detection changed, model may overrun and append extra text.
4) Data drift in tuning set: v1.9 training data may include more examples where assistants invent features — check training diff (PR #2138 referenced below).

Immediate triage steps (what I did / to do):
- Re-ran 20 deterministic prompts with temperature=0 and same max_tokens to isolate stochasticity — hallucinations persisted on ~6 prompts.
- Compared decode args between v1.8 and v1.9 (local config dump) — found that v1.9 had new presence_penalty default of 0.2; need to test disabling.
- Opened Linear ticket REDW-4824 to capture customer-impacting regression.
- TODO: run focused set of 200 format-sensitive prompts (JSON, yaml, CSV) across batch sizes.
- TODO: add unit test that asserts no new keys for strict-JSON prompts.

Notes to self / heuristics I want to remember:
- When evaluating assistant hallucination, create a short checklist: verify (1) claim is checkable, (2) cross-check with product docs (links), (3) mark as 'plausible but not verified' if ambiguous.
- Keep a separate small corpus of 'format-only' prompts for smoke tests. These catch subtle decode behavior changes quickly.
- If a regression is configuration-level (decode args), look for rollback-first fix while deeper tuning happens.

Links / references:
- PR for v1.9 release notes: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/2138
- Triage ticket: https://linear.app/REDW/issue/REDW-4824
- Internal slack: #eng-applied-ml thread "v1.9-format-regressions" (searchable)

Next steps (short horizon):
- Reproduce at scale on dedicated infra (to rule out local runner differences) by 2026-03-12.
- If decode arg change confirmed, ship temporary config override on hosted to force previous decode defaults.
- If model-level behavior confirmed, escalate to model-onboarding/research for a delta-minimization patch or rollback.

Closing note: this doc is a working scratchpad — copy notes into REDW-4824 and the release notes checklist once findings are finalized. Keep the sample prompts here for quick smoke-test re-runs.
plain_text_summary: Short scratchpad capturing ad-hoc rubric and regression observations comparing v1.8 vs v1.9 — main issues: increased hallucinations and format violations in v1.9. Next actions: confirm decode args, run larger smoke tests, and file fixes/rollbacks.
